output.premise: Generations ago, humanity descended into a vast cavern network to escape something on the surface—something the ruling merchant guilds refuse to discuss. Now the underground city of stillwater_hollow is slowly drowning. Water rises year by year, flooding the lower districts and forcing thousands upward into overcrowded, guild-controlled terraces. The guilds hold power through monopoly: they own the pumps, the salvage routes to the sealed surface gates, the filtered water, and the archive of what came before. They claim the surface is poisoned, uninhabitable, dead. Most believe them, because believing otherwise means admitting the guilds have been lying for a century. But the pumps are failing, the salvage is running thin, and the water keeps rising. Something has to change—reform, revolt, or a desperate expedition upward—but every path costs something someone cannot afford to lose.
themes: Scarcity as a tool of control
Hope as a dangerous and finite resource

faction_seeds: The Compact of Tides: Coalition of the three wealthiest merchant guilds who jointly govern Stillwater Hollow through permits, water rights, and control of the historical archive; they maintain that the surface is dead and the city's slow drowning is manageable.

The Stillwell Brotherhood: Guild controlling the ancient pumps and water filtration; their engineers know the systems are failing but fear that public knowledge would trigger panic and revolt, so they ration quietly and search desperately for solutions.

The Lampwrights Guild: Controllers of all artificial light in the habitable zones; their monopoly on illumination makes them indispensable and gives them outsized political influence despite their smaller size.
The Drowned: Not a formal faction but a growing underclass of flood-refugees from the lower wards; organized informally, increasingly radical, and beginning to demand representation or retribution.

The Surface Seekers: Loose network of scavengers, scholars, and dreamers who believe the surface may be habitable again; they seek evidence, smuggle salvage, and quietly plan expeditions the guilds would punish severely.

The Vowkeepers: Remnant religious order preserving fragments of pre-Descent records and oral histories; they hold pieces of the truth about why humanity fled but are divided on whether revelation would save or destroy the city.

The Siltwater Smugglers: Black-market network moving unlicensed goods, people, and information between wards; pragmatic survivors who profit from the guilds' restrictions and would lose everything if the system reformed too quickly.
tensions: The pumps are failing faster than the Stillwell Brotherhood admits; each month brings new breakdowns, and the guilds refuse to invest in full repair because acknowledging the crisis means acknowledging the city may be unsustainable.
The Drowned demand dry ground and representation; the guilds offer token charity and relocation to worse housing, pushing thousands toward radicalization.
Surface Seekers have found anomalies suggesting the surface may not be as dead as the guilds claim, but proving it requires an expedition the guilds will arrest anyone for attempting.
The Vowkeepers possess documents that contradict the official history of the Descent, but releasing them could destabilize the city; some members want to burn the records to prevent chaos.
Guild quota disputes are strangling the Glassworks and the Vats; production is falling, food is scarce, and the guilds would rather suppress output data than redistribute power.
The Siltwater Smugglers are becoming the Drowned's real infrastructure; if the guilds crack down, they risk triggering open revolt, but tolerating them erodes guild authority.
The Sealed Gates are showing signs of deterioration from the surface side—stress fractures, temperature changes, sounds—raising questions about what, if anything, is pressing to get in or out.

Reformists within the guilds argue for gradual power-sharing to prevent revolution; hardliners argue that any concession will be read as weakness and invite collapse; both sides are right about the other's plan failing.

locations.name: Drowned Exchange
locations.description: A half-submerged trading hall built into the ruins of a pre-flood bank vault, where the Salt Ledger conducts its business. The upper galleries remain dry and are reserved for those with positive air credit. The lower floors are flooded knee-to-chest deep, where desperate traders wade to barter salvage, labor contracts, and minutes of breathable air. Massive vault doors now serve as bulkheads against the rising water. The air here is thick with brine and the whispers of those negotiating terms that may never be settled. Every transaction adds to someone's debt, and the Ledger's clerks watch from catwalks above, recording everything in brine-stained ledgers.

locations.name: The Last Pump
locations.description: The ancient mechanism that keeps the lower vaults from complete inundation, and it is dying. The Pump Wardens tend it with a mixture of engineering and desperate ritual, replacing corroded parts with salvaged metal and prayer. Each day the pump's rhythm grows more irregular. When it stops, the lower levels flood within hours, and the air pressure that keeps the upper galleries breathable begins to equalize. The Wardens know the pump needs parts that may no longer exist in the flooded city, and they are running out of ways to patch both the machinery and the truth. The chamber echoes with the laboring groan of metal that has outlasted its builders.

factions: Salt Ledger — The dominant merchant guild, so named for the brine-stained ledgers that record every citizen's air debt. They control the distribution of filtered air and access to the few remaining dry platforms. Their authority rests on a simple premise: without the Ledger's records and infrastructure, everyone drowns. They are not cruel for cruelty's sake; they believe rationing is survival and that debt is the only system that keeps people working toward collective preservation. But the Ledger is also a bureaucracy that has forgotten mercy, where a child's breathing allowance can be garnished for a parent's unpaid labor, and where the surface and its abandonment are questions no clerk is permitted to ask aloud.

Pump Wardens — The engineers and mechanics who keep the city's pumps running. Once a respected craft guild, they are now a desperate order maintaining failing machinery with dwindling expertise. Many elder Wardens have died or retired, and the knowledge transfer is incomplete. They know the Last Pump is failing and disagree sharply on the response: some want to openly petition the Salt Ledger for resources and risk panic; others want to cannibalize secondary pumps to buy time; a few whisper that the abandoned surface might hold salvageable parts, if anyone could survive the climb. Their loyalty is to the machinery and the people it keeps alive, not to the Ledger that rationed their predecessors to death.
tensions: Air debt — The Salt Ledger's system of air rationing binds every citizen to labor they may never finish paying off. The debt is inheritable, creating generational servitude that sparks quiet resistance, desperate bargains, and a growing underground of people who trade favors outside the Ledger's records. Some argue the debt system is the only thing preventing chaos; others see it as a cage that will drown them all slowly.

A failing pump — The Last Pump's deterioration threatens to flood the lower vaults and collapse air pressure throughout the city. The Pump Wardens' internal disagreements about how to respond mirror the larger question facing everyone: can the city be saved through salvage and sacrifice, or is it time to seek another way, even if that means confronting what the guilds have hidden about the surface?

output.secret_plot:
THE TRUTH: The surface was sealed deliberately by Salt Ledger founders three generations ago. It is not toxic—it is habitable, perhaps recovering. The underground city exists because merchants engineered a containment crisis to create a captive population dependent on controlled air. The air-debt economy is built on manufactured scarcity.

THE LAST PUMP: Its deeper mechanisms, understood only by senior Pump Wardens, can open the great seal to the surface. The pump is failing because Salt Ledger agents have quietly degraded it for years—ensuring the seal cannot open even if discovered. The crisis is sabotage dressed as decay.

SALT LEDGER SPLIT: The Inner Circle (founder descendants) knows the truth and maintains the lie. Reformists suspect the surface may be viable but lack proof. Hardliners know the truth and want the pump destroyed—fearing reopening will destroy their order.

PUMP WARDEN DOUBT: Senior Warden Cael Murk has identified tool marks on the pump's seal mechanisms indicating deliberate sabotage, not age. He hasn't shared this widely. Wardens are split: some believe him, some think he's pressure-sick, some are co-opted by Hardliners.

CLUES: (1) Tool marks on the pump's seal mechanisms—deliberate, inconsistent with wear. (2) The Drowned Exchange holds waterlogged archives referencing 'the Compact of Containment' and payments to 'surface sealers' from the founding generation. (3) Air readings near the upper seal show compositions inconsistent with the toxic-surface narrative; the Salt Ledger suppresses them. (4) A dying founder's confession, sealed in a vault beneath the Drowned Exchange, names three conspirators and admits the surface was 'not yet dead.' The vault key is held by a Salt Ledger elder. (5) Pump Warden initiates learn a ritual phrase about 'the breath above'—actually a fragment of the surface-opening protocol.

PATH ONE—REFORM: Ally with Reformists and sympathetic Wardens for a controlled reopening. Cost: air-debt economy collapses, debtors revolt, Hardliners attempt to destroy the pump. The surface is habitable but not welcoming—no infrastructure. Hope, but expensive.

PATH TWO—SEIZURE: Side with Murk and militant Wardens to seize the pump by force, demanding truth and opening. Cost: open conflict with Salt Ledger enforcers. The pump is vulnerable during fighting—damage could doom everyone. If successful, the surface opens but underground order shatters. Wardens are mechanics, not governors.

CONSEQUENCES: If truth is revealed and nothing changes, Salt Ledger legitimacy erodes and unrest grows. If the pump fails before the seal opens, everyone dies. If the surface opens, the underground city may be abandoned within a generation, but the transition will be brutal. No path is without cost, but there are paths.

locations.name: The Drowned Exchange
locations.description: A vast submerged hall where merchants conduct trade from gondolas and half-flooded platforms. The upper galleries remain dry, reserved for guild lords who breathe the city's most precious commodity: compressed air. Below the waterline, divers retrieve lost goods from drowned storehouses. Every transaction is recorded in the Salt Ledger's waterproof ledgers, and every breath taken in the Exchange adds to a trader's air debt. The Exchange is the economic heart of the city, where hope and desperation are bought and sold in equal measure.

locations.name: The Last Pump
locations.description: A colossal machine of brass and iron that groans day and night, keeping the lower districts from complete inundation. The Pump Wardens tend it with religious devotion, performing rituals of maintenance passed down through generations. Water seeps through every seal, and the pump's rhythm falters more each month. Should it fail, the remaining dry districts will flood within hours. The Wardens hoard replacement parts and knowledge, making access to the Pump a matter of political negotiation as much as mechanical necessity.

factions: Salt Ledger: The guild of record-keepers, accountants, and debt-collectors who track every exchange of air, goods, and labor in the city. Their waterproof ledgers are the law, and their enforcers ensure that no debt goes unpaid. They control the issuance of air credits, the currency of survival. While they present themselves as neutral arbiters, their records hold the secrets of the city's origins and the reason the surface was abandoned. They trade in information as readily as air, and their archives are the most complete source of history in the flooded world.

Pump Wardens: The engineers, mechanics, and operators who keep The Last Pump running. They are a closed order, passing down technical knowledge through apprenticeship and refusing to share their secrets. They control access to the pump and thus to the dry ground that remains. Some say they could fix the pump permanently if they chose; others say they are barely holding it together with salvaged parts and desperate ingenuity. Their power comes from their monopoly on survival, and they use it to extract concessions from the other guilds. They know that if the pump fails, their relevance dies with it, but they will not surrender their leverage cheaply.
tensions: Air debt: The city runs on a system of air credits. Every citizen is born with a debt for the air they will breathe, and every action that consumes air — from walking to a meeting to operating a forge — accrues interest. Those who cannot pay are exiled to the flooded lower levels or have their air supply cut off. The Salt Ledger administers this system with cold precision, but the ledger's origins are murky, and some suspect the air debt was invented to control the population rather than manage scarce resources. Agitating against the system is treason, but whispers of a surface where air is free grow louder.

A failing pump: The Last Pump is dying. Its rhythm falters, its seals weep, and its core temperature rises despite the Wardens' best efforts. Replacement parts are scarce; the knowledge to build new ones was lost when the surface was sealed. The Wardens claim they can keep it running indefinitely with proper resources and respect, but the signs of decay are undeniable. When the pump fails — not if, but when — the city will drown. Some factions hoard boats and diving equipment. Others search the archives for forgotten technologies. A few pray for a miracle. The question is not whether the pump will fail, but who will be on high ground when it does.

output.secret_plot:
THE FOUNDERS' SIN

**Core Secret:** The surface was not abandoned due to an uncontrollable cataclysm. It was deliberately poisoned by the founding merchant guilds (ancestors of the Salt Ledger) to create a captive market for air and water. They sabotaged the **Deep Lung**—the original atmospheric processor—and sealed the surface exits, fabricating the story of "The Sundering" to justify their rule.

**Where the Truth Lies:** The evidence is hidden in the **Founders' Vault**, a sealed chamber beneath the **Drowned Exchange**. It contains the original Deep Lung schematics, the signed sabotage orders, and a functional surface communication device.

**Faction Motives & Secrets:**
- **Salt Ledger (Grand Factor Orin Vask):** Knows the truth. Maintains the lie to keep the Air Debt system running. Has been secretly diverting resources to build a private air-scrubbing **Citadel** for the elite, accelerating the Last Pump's decay.
- **Pump Wardens (Master Warden Elara Moss):** Suspects the Salt Ledger is lying. A secret cell of **Deep Wardens** has been mapping the Exchange's sub-basements, searching for the Vault to save the Pump. They don't know the full truth yet, only that the Ledger is sabotaging repairs.

**Discoverable Clues:**
1. **The Dying Warden's Map:** A dying Deep Warden gives the party a wax-stained map of the **Exchange Undercroft**, marked with a strange seal (the Founders' Key). The seal matches the Grand Factor's ring.
2. **The Forged Component:** While repairing the Last Pump's main piston, a Warden finds a bronze valve stamped with a date 50 years after the official Sundering. It was made on the surface. This proves the surface was habitable long after the lie began.
3. **The Uncancelled Debt:** A tax ledger from the Drowned Exchange lists a standing, interest-accruing debt from the "City of Ember" (the surface colony) to the "Guild Primeval" (the founders). The debt is for "Atmospheric Genocide Restitution." The interest is due, but the principal was never collected because the debtors were the ones who committed the crime.
4. **The Grand Factor's Panic:** If the party gets too close, Vask offers a massive bribe (forgiveness of all Air Debt + a position in the Citadel) to drop the investigation. Refusal triggers an assassination attempt using Salt Ledger Enforcers and a staged pump failure.

**Escalation Paths:**
- **Path 1: The Revelation.** The party opens the Founders' Vault and broadcasts the truth via the Exchange's resonance speakers. Cost: The Salt Ledger enforces martial law. The Pump is sabotaged in the chaos. The party must lead a revolution while simultaneously preventing the city from suffocating. Hope: A free city, but built on the ashes of the old order.
- **Path 2: The Fix.** The party uses the secret to blackmail Vask. He is forced to fund the Pump repairs and ease the Air Debt. Cost: The party becomes the secret police of the lie, executing anyone who gets too close to the truth. The surface remains abandoned. Hope: The city survives sustainably, and the party slowly reforms the system, but they must become monsters to do it.
- **Path 3: The Exodus.** The party uses the Vault's schematics to recalibrate the Deep Lung. They can make the surface habitable for a small group (100-200 people). Cost: The recalibration drains the city's remaining air reserves for a full day, causing mass casualties. The Salt Ledger fights to stop them. Hope: A new beginning for a chosen few, leaving the rest to the fate the founders created.

output.premise: The city of Lumenmere sprawls through flooded limestone caverns, its districts linked by a lattice of canals and leaky pressure-gates. For centuries the merchant guilds have ruled from floating bazaars and dripping promenades, their wealth built on salvaged surface-world relics. They preach that the sun above is a killing fire and that submersion is salvation. In truth, the surface was not abandoned by nature but poisoned by a desperate act of their ancestors — a blight seeded in the soil to halt an advancing enemy, which instead crept downward into the groundwater. Now the city’s lower levels are dying from the rising Depth Blight, a slow corruption that distorts flesh and mind. The guilds hoard the secret, ration oxygen-fungus and light, and trade in human desperation. Yet in the choked vents and sunken archives, fragments of the old sin surface, and a handful of voices whisper that the surface may not be dead — only waiting, and vengeful.

location_seeds.name: The Bazaar Afloat

faction_seeds: The Silt Council: the oligarchy of oldest merchant families who control water-cleaners, oxygen-fungus quotas, and the relic trade. They believe only rigid order and selective ignorance prevent complete collapse, and they will sacrifice whole districts to maintain that order.

The Lamplighter's Union: hereditary keepers of the Guttering Spire, possessing secret techniques to coax light from dying spores. They are the closest thing to a neutral security force, but their loyalty is strained by dwindling resources and the Council's disregard for their needs.

The Depth-Dredgers: a loose guild of salvagers who brave the Blighted depths for powerful pre-Fall artifacts. They live short, lucrative lives, and many form strange cults around the things they find. They trade in a currency called 'glimmer' that is both valuables and addictive story-echoes.

The Archivists: an ancient order that preserves the memory-codices and keeps the original Blight records sealed. They know the truth and are riven between those who feel the secret must be kept for stability and those who believe the city deserves to know before it drowns in corruption.

The Guttered: the disenfranchised masses of the Canal Warrens and Husk Markets. They have no formal organization, but charismatic preachers and Blight-survivors sometimes rally them into short-lived revolts. Their very desperation makes them a tool for any faction willing to pay in food or light.

The Spore-Cutters: a ruthless biotech cartel that cultivates the oxygen-fungus on floating platforms. They experiment on Debtbound to develop Blight-resistant strains, and they control the air supply more directly than the Council admits. Whispered to be feeding something in the depths.
tensions: The Guttering Spire dims perceptibly each cycle, and the Lamplighter's Union demands a full tithe of salvaged energy-cells to restore it. The Silt Council diverts those cells to keep the Barrier Locks operational, pitting light against safety.

A new strain of Depth Blight spreads upward from the Deep Roots, causing nightmares and water-births before physical distortion. The Council debates sealing the lower Warrens forever—trapping thousands inside with the infection.

The Archivists possess a recently decoded memory-codex that shows the surface was not instant death but a slow-blooming garden of toxic mourning. Releasing this would shatter the guilds' founding lie but might also reveal a pathway to a surface cure.

A charismatic Surface-Seeker called the Echo claims to have found a dry, breathable cave near the surface. Their followers are vanishing from the city, but no one returns, and the Council fears a mass exodus into certain death—or worse, success.

The Spore-Cutters threaten to halt oxygen-fungus production unless granted control of the Engine Ward, where a new breed could be grown in the thermal runoff. This would make the city's entire breathable air supply a single cartel's property.

The Depth-Dredgers have begun trading 'salt-echoes,' memories extracted from pre-Fall skulls that show flashes of the surface before the Blight. These echoes are instantly contraband under Council law, but they spread like wildfire through the Warrens, seeding discontent and madness.

locations.name: Drowned Exchange

Merchants in skiffs trade air-credits, salvage, and pump-parts beneath a cracked dome that drips rust-stained water. locations.name: The Last Pump

Sacrificial 'pump-feeds' are lowered into the gear-wells to clear blockages, their air rations donated to the Wardens. The walls sweat condensation that tastes faintly of copper and old blood.

locations.name: Breath Vault
locations.description: A sealed, high-ceilinged chamber where the city's air is compressed and stored in corroded brass tanks. The Salt Ledger holds the keys, and armed auditors patrol the catwalks. Citizens come here to pay their air-debt, receiving stamped chits that permit breathing in the habitable zones. The vault's hum is punctuated by the coughs of those whose credit has run dry. A small shrine to the 'First Breather' stands in the corner, draped in faded ribbons—a reminder that air was once free.

locations.name: Sump Warrens

Air here is stale and often unregistered—those without chits breathe illegally, risking the Salt Ledger's enforcers. locations.name: Guildhall Spire
locations.description: A slender tower of riveted iron rising from the dry heart of the city, seat of the Salt Ledger. Its upper levels are richly appointed with salvaged surface relics—cracked porcelain, faded tapestries—and the air is sweetened by rare filtration sachets. Ledger-keepers in grey robes calculate breath-debts on clicking brass engines. Deals that shape the city's fate are made here, often sealed with a pint of blood and a new entry in the great debt-ledger. The basement holds the 'Silent Cells', where defaulters are left to contemplate their airless futures.

locations.name: Gutter Gate
locations.description: A massive, rust-streaked portcullis that bars passage to the fully flooded lower levels. Water seeps through in constant rivulets, and the air is heavy with the mineral tang of deep earth. Pump Wardens maintain a watchpost here, but the gate is also a gathering point for scavengers and exiles preparing to dive into the sunken districts. Beyond lies the Drowned City—shattered spires and silent archives that hide pre-flood secrets. Whispers say something moves down there, stirring in the dark water.

locations.name: Surface Seal
locations.description: A circular hatch of blackened metal set in the highest dome of the vault, surrounded by warning glyphs and the faded insignia of the old builders. The Seal Keepers—a mute order of masked guardians—maintain a permanent vigil, their oaths passed down through generations. No one alive has seen the surface; records claim it is poison, a wasteland of choking fog. Yet sometimes, during the pump's deepest groans, a faint draft slips through the seal, carrying a scent that is neither rot nor rust—something almost green.

locations.name: Churnworks
locations.description: A sprawling industrial chamber where water from the sumps is filtered through layers of charcoal, sand, and salvaged membranes. The Churnworks are operated by the Pump Wardens' engineering caste, who maintain a precarious balance—too much filtration slows the pumps, too little poisons the habitable zones. Workers wear heavy respirators against the chemical stink, and accidents are common. The filtered sludge is pressed into 'mud-bricks' used for construction, each brick flecked with the rust of ancient machinery.

output.premise: The city of Drenchspire was never meant to be a city at all — it was a refuge, a mine, a last resort. When the surface was abandoned three centuries ago, tens of thousands fled into the carved-out depths beneath the mountain, sealing the Vault-Locks behind them. The official histories speak of a blight, a slow poison in the air and soil that made the surface uninhabitable. The lower districts drown inch by inch. And the Gatekeepers — the only faction permitted near the surface seals — have stopped answering questions about what they hear scratching on the other side. In Drenchspire, everything has a price, including the truth. And nobody can afford it.

locations.name: Drowned Exchange
locations.description: A sprawling trade platform suspended on rusted chains above black, still water in the city's central vault. Merchants of the Salt Ledger conduct business from iron cages hung at varying heights — the higher the cage, the more prestigious the trader. Light comes from phosphorescent fungal lanterns that gutter and dim unpredictably. The air here is thick with mildew and whispered negotiations. Every transaction is recorded in salt-tablet ledgers, and a missed payment can mean relocation to the lower, wetter tiers. Beneath the platform, in the dark water, debtors sometimes float reminders of what is owed.

locations.name: The Last Pump
locations.description: A cathedral-sized machine of corroded brass and groaning pistons that stands at the lowest still-habitable level of the city. It is the sole remaining pump keeping the deeper vaults from flooding entirely, and it has run without pause for longer than anyone can remember. The Pump Wardens maintain it with dwindling parts and improvised repairs, and its rhythm — a deep, shuddering thump that echoes through every chamber — is the heartbeat of the city. When it skips, everyone notices. The Wardens have walled off the pump chamber from casual access, and those who enter speak of a sound like something breathing on the other side of the intake pipes.

locations.name: The Dry Stacks
locations.description: Tiered residential galleries carved into the highest surviving vault walls, where the air is warmest and the damp recedes. Living space here is the most coveted asset in the city, allocated by guild standing and air-debt rating. The upper tiers house Salt Ledger officers and senior Wardens in relative comfort, with private air-scrubbers and mushroom gardens. The middle tiers shelter skilled laborers and their families in cramped but stable quarters. The lowest habitable rows are perpetually clammy, their residents one missed payment from relocation to the flooded levels below. Access between tiers is controlled by locked stairwells and guild enforcers.

locations.name: The Sealed Gate
locations.description: A colossal bulkhead of scarred metal set into the highest vault ceiling, marking the route the ancestors used when they descended. Its locking mechanism is a frozen mass of rust and calcified seals, untouched for generations. The Salt Ledger maintains a permanent guard post here — officially to prevent tampering, unofficially to discourage questions. A faded warning is still visible on the gate's surface in a language few can still read. The Gate-Seekers believe old maintenance tunnels bypass the lock, but exploring them means venturing into flooded sections where no guild authority reaches.

locations.name: The Sump Markets
locations.description: A floating black market built on lashed-together rafts and flooded walkways in the deepest accessible chambers. Here the Breathless and the desperate trade outside the Salt Ledger's ledgers: stolen air tokens, salvaged machine parts, surface relics of unknown purpose, and less tangible commodities like silence, loyalty, and memory. The water is shallow enough to wade through but deep enough to hide what sinks. The Salt Ledger publicly condemns the Sump Markets while maintaining a network of informants and cutouts who ensure a percentage of every trade flows upward. Light here comes from bioluminescent fungi cultivated by the Breathless — a cold, blue glow.

locations.name: The Counting Dark
locations.description: The Salt Ledger's central record hall and treasury, a windowless chamber suspended by chains above the deepest water in the city. Here, every air-debt ever incurred is recorded on salt tablets stacked in floor-to-ceiling racks. The air is deliberately kept thin and cold — the Ledger's clerks claim it sharpens the mind, but it also ensures no visitor stays longer than necessary. The oldest tablets in the lowest racks are said to record the original debt: the price the ancestors paid to seal the city. Those racks are kept locked, and their keys are held by no single person.

locations.name: The Grateworks
locations.description: A vast industrial chamber where ancient filtration systems cycle the city's atmosphere through immense beds of cultivated fungus. The air that emerges is breathable but carries a permanent earthy staleness that every citizen knows as the taste of home. The Grateworks are operated by a hereditary workforce who wear breathing masks not for protection but as a guild tradition — they claim to remember what unfiltered air smelled like. Maintenance is falling behind; three of the twelve primary grates have seized shut, and the remaining nine run at dangerous capacity. A full grate failure would render the upper vaults unbreathable within days.

factions: Salt Ledger: The merchant guild that created and controls the air-debt system. They track every breath loaned and every obligation owed with meticulous precision, maintaining power through debt enforcement, trade monopoly, and the implicit threat of relocation to the flooded depths. They see themselves as the city's necessary order — without them, they argue, the vaults would descend into chaos and drowning. Their leadership is gerontocratic and opaque; major decisions are made by a council whose membership is itself a closely held secret. The Ledger's greatest fear is not rebellion but audit: someone proving the debt system is a fiction.

Pump Wardens: The engineers, mechanics, and laborers who maintain the Last Pump and the city's remaining water control infrastructure. Their irreplaceable expertise gives them the only leverage that matters against the Salt Ledger — the credible threat of a work stoppage. They are organized as a guild but increasingly fractured: Pragmatists want negotiated reform, Hardliners want to seize control of the city by weaponizing the pump, and a growing Exodus faction wants to abandon the vaults entirely and redirect all resources toward opening the Sealed Gate. The Wardens know the pump's true condition and the timeline is shorter than anyone admits.

The Breathless: Those who have defaulted on their air-debt and been exiled to the lowest, partially flooded levels. The player characters can expose the truth through the Drowned Exchange vault, follow illegal maintenance routes to the Last Pump, or compare Salt Ledger accounts with Warden pressure records. Each discovery forces a choice rather than providing a clean victory. One escalation path is reform: publish the evacuation records, break the guild monopoly, and organize voluntary labor and rationing to stabilize the engine. This preserves many lives but causes immediate shortages, riots, and likely loss of the surface’s remaining dry infrastructure. A second path is rupture: help the Wardens shut down the engine or redirect it to flood the merchant districts. This ends the air debt and may free the city from its founding injustice, but thousands could die before survivors reach the surface. A third, compromised path is concealment and expansion: support the Salt Ledger in hiding the truth while reopening selected surface pumps, buying time at the cost of deepening exploitation and making a later failure far worse. The hidden plot’s central secret is that the engine can be dismantled and rebuilt, but only if the factions surrender their claims, the city accepts a season of scarcity, and the players persuade enemies who each possess one indispensable part of the original design. Hope is possible, but every route makes someone pay for the choices that created the city.

issues: The secret plot directly contradicts the public fact that no route to the surface exists: a weekly caravan requires a viable route and access.
The secret plot also contradicts the premise that the surface has been unreachable for ages; regular guild caravans demonstrate ongoing reachability.
The guild's weekly surface activity is a dangling, unexplained reference: no route, means, or concealment mechanism is supplied to reconcile it with public knowledge.
The contradiction undermines the stated premise and the central mystery of why the surface was abandoned, so the world is not safe to publish without correction.

output.premise: Nethertide is a colossal subterranean cistern-city built into the walls of a lightless cavern, now half-submerged by a rising, toxic-looking black water. The surface is officially declared a dead, irradiated wasteland, a myth used to maintain order. In truth, the surface was abandoned due to a manageable but politically inconvenient ecological collapse, and the ruling merchant guilds sealed the gates to monopolize the underground's finite clean air and water. Survival in Nethertide is dictated by verticality: the elite live in the dry, well-lit upper tiers, while the poor drown in the silt-choked lower warrens. The darkness stems not from arbitrary evil, but from a brutally rational economic system where every breath of filtered air and every drop of clean water is commodified. Meaningful agency exists through sabotage, smuggling, engineering, and uncovering the past, but every action to change the system carries a heavy, often fatal, cost to the fragile ecosystem keeping the city from total inundation.

location_seeds.name: The Rust Terraces
location_seeds.purpose: Mid-level slums built on corroded scaffolding. Constant threat of structural collapse, but the only place where unlicensed scavengers can trade surface artifacts and black-market air filters.

location_seeds.name: Pump Station Alpha
location_seeds.purpose: The primary water purification and air-circulation hub. Heavily fortified by the ruling guilds; control of the pumps means control of the city's lifeblood and the ultimate leverage over the populace.

location_seeds.name: The Drowned Archives
location_seeds.purpose: A partially submerged repository of pre-flood history. Accessible only by skilled divers, it holds the suppressed truth of the surface abandonment and the original blueprints of the city's seals.

location_seeds.name: Gilded Drydocks
location_seeds.purpose: The exclusive upper-tier docks where guild elite reside safely above the high-water mark. A hub of opulent trade and political maneuvering, built entirely on the backs of indentured divers.

location_seeds.name: The Silt Warrens
location_seeds.purpose: The lowest habitable tier, constantly battling the rising black water. Home to the desperate, the exiled, and radical factions. A place of drowning shadows and failing bulkheads.

faction_seeds: The Hydro-Barons: A cartel of merchant guilds that monopolize water purification and air scrubbers, maintaining power through artificial scarcity, debt-peonage, and controlling the historical narrative.
The Dredge-Runners: Smugglers and scavengers who navigate the flooded lower levels, trading in contraband, pre-flood tech, and dangerous secrets for those willing to pay their steep prices.
The Tide-Callers: A fatalistic cult in the Silt Warrens that believes the flood is a divine cleansing ritual. They actively sabotage the pumps and bulkheads to hasten the city's purification.

The Iron-Lung Syndicate: Engineers and mechanics who maintain the failing infrastructure. They hold the city together physically, but are increasingly radicalized by the guilds' refusal to provide better rations.

The Surface Seekers: A clandestine network of scholars and divers trying to uncover the truth about the surface. They seek to restore the world above, but lack the resources to challenge the Barons directly.
tensions: The primary pumps are failing, requiring increasingly dangerous dives to salvage parts, pushing the lower tiers to the brink of drowning while the Barons hoard the remaining functional tech.
The Hydro-Barons are deliberately flooding lower sectors to drive up the price of dry real estate and air credits, forcing the poor into indentured servitude to afford survival.

Dredge-Runners have found pre-flood tech proving the surface is habitable, but revealing it would shatter the guilds' monopoly and cause a violent uprising that could destroy the fragile life-support systems.
The Tide-Callers are gaining recruits among the drowning poor, threatening to destroy Pump Station Alpha in a mass sacrifice that would suffocate the upper tiers.
The Iron-Lung Syndicate is on the verge of a general strike, which would halt air circulation and kill thousands, forcing players to choose between supporting the workers or preventing a massacre.

locations.name: Drowned Exchange
locations.description: A sprawling, half-submerged bazaar built into the rusted catwalks of the vault-city's upper tiers. Here, the merchant guilds dictate the price of breathable air and dry standing room. Traders barter in pressurized canisters, moisture-seals, and indentured favors. The dark water constantly laps at the lower stalls, quietly claiming the livelihoods of those who fall behind on their debts. Despite the oppressive atmosphere, it remains the only place to find smuggled surface artifacts, forge illicit alliances, or negotiate a costly path out of poverty.

locations.name: The Last Pump
locations.description: A colossal, deafening geothermal engine at the city's lowest accessible point, tasked with pushing the rising subterranean sea back into the deep aquifers. The Pump Wardens live in the sweltering, oil-slicked catwalks surrounding it, sacrificing their health and hearing to keep the massive pistons firing. The machinery is failing, groaning under centuries of neglect, and its irregular shudders directly dictate the rising water levels in the lower wards. Keeping it running requires rare parts and desperate dives into the flooded sectors, offering a dangerous but vital path to buy the city more time.

output.secret_plot: The surface was not abandoned due to a natural cataclysm; the ancestors of the Salt Ledger intentionally breached the ancient seawalls to drown the surface, trapping the populace underground to establish an absolute monopoly on dry land and breathable air. The Last Pump is not failing from age, but from deliberate sabotage. The Salt Ledger has been cannibalizing its vital components to construct the sub-aquatic vaults of the Drowned Exchange, using the resulting Air debt crisis to harvest desperate labor and consolidate power. The Pump Wardens have secretly uncovered the original seawall breaching logs and the sabotaged pump mechanics. Clues surface through discrepancies in the Drowned Exchange public repair manifests, which show massive expenditures for pump parts that were actually diverted to vault construction. At The Last Pump, Wardens find original surface-sea wall blueprints hidden in the maintenance shafts, alongside inferior alloy replacements that guarantee eventual failure. This secret enables two plausible escalation paths driven by player choices. Path 1, The Wardens Deluge: The Pump Wardens weaponize the failing pump to intentionally flood the Drowned Exchange, destroying the Salt Ledger physical debt records and vaults. However, this requires players to manually hold the secondary valves open, risking the drowning of the lower tiers unless they can secure a costly, temporary air-pact with a rival merchant faction. Path 2, The Ledger Purge: The Salt Ledger discovers the Wardens mutiny and uses Air debt enforcers to seize The Last Pump. They plan to vent the lower levels into the toxic floodwaters to save air for the upper tiers. Players must choose between sacrificing the lower levels to secure a hidden passage to the now-habitable surface, or remaining in the city to defend the pump, accepting a grueling, costly war of attrition to reclaim the underground.

issues: The premise and public facts state as objective reality that the surface is unreachable and no route exists, which directly contradicts the secret plot of the guild sending a weekly caravan to the surface. The public facts must be reframed as false public beliefs or enforced dogma rather than objective world truths to resolve this contradiction.
